review_notes: I read the whole file and checked its simp interface. Nothing in it carries @[simp]. The top of the file is a `attribute [-simp]` block that removes simp lemmas defined elsewhere, which I treated as infrastructure. I looked for missing canonical simp lemmas and for competing or duplicated rewrite forms. I compared against the Definitions file where Place.evalAt is defined and grepped the repository for other copies of evalAt_zero. I could not run Lean. The second finding is lower confidence: it depends on how simp discharges the `hDt` side condition, and I did not check that experimentally. I did not flag wq_apply, regVal_apply, evalVec_apply or nsmul_two_add_apply. They are unfolding lemmas used by `rw`, and making them simp lemmas would expand the pivot definitions or add little.

findings.excerpt: theorem evalAt_zero (Q : Place K F) : Q.evalAt (0 : F) = 0 := by
findings.problem: `Place.evalAt 0 = 0` is the obvious companion of `Place.evalAt_one`, which is `@[simp]` in the defining file. Here it is a plain, unattributed theorem in the P2MW namespace rather than `Place.evalAt_zero`. Every use is a manual `exact evalAt_zero Q` or `rw [..., evalAt_zero]`. The same lemma is re-proved under the names `evalAt_zero` and `evalAt_zero'` in at least four other P2M/Sol files, which signals that the canonical simp lemma is missing from the definitions file. Because there is no simp lemma, goals like `Q.evalAt (0 * x)` or `Q.evalAt (c • 0)` do not normalise, and the `empty` cases in `evalAt_sum_smul_of_mem` need `simp only [Finset.sum_empty]; exact evalAt_zero Q`.
findings.proposed_change: Move the lemma next to `Place.evalAt_one` in Definitions/Def_AlgebraicCurve_PlaceEvaluation(Algebra) as `@[simp] theorem Place.evalAt_zero (v : Place K F) : v.evalAt (0 : F) = 0`. Its proof is the existing one: apply `evalAt_algebraMap_eq 0` and rewrite with `map_zero`. In this file, drop the local copy and replace `exact evalAt_zero Q` and `rw [..., evalAt_zero]` with `simp`. That includes the `empty` case of `evalAt_sum_smul_of_mem`, the `hwr0` step and the `hg0` branch of `regVal_chord_eq_evalAt_wr`.
findings.benefit: The zero case is handled by `simp` in one place. This removes the repeated local re-proofs (`evalAt_zero'` in several files). Simp normal forms then agree with `evalAt_one`, and no call site has to name the lemma.

findings.declaration: P2MW.der_zero / der_one / der_algebraMap / der_self / der_add / der_sub / der_smul
findings.excerpt: theorem der_zero {t : F} (hDt : D K F t ≠ 0) : der K t (0 : F) = 0 := by
findings.problem: `der K t` behaves as a derivation under the hypothesis `D K F t ≠ 0`. The file proves the full set of rewrite rules for it (`der_zero`, `der_one`, `der_algebraMap`, `der_self`, `der_add`, `der_sub`, `der_mul`, `der_smul`), but none is a simp lemma. All call sites therefore use manual `rw [der_mul hDt, der_self hDt]; ring`, or `simp only [Finset.sum_empty]; exact der_zero hDt`, and re-pass `hDt` each time. There is no `simp [hDt]` route to normalise `der K t (a • g - b • f)`, `der K t (t * g)` and similar terms. The hand-written `der_smul_sub_smul` exists only to bundle such a rewrite.
findings.proposed_change: Tag the conditional rules `der_zero`, `der_one`, `der_algebraMap`, `der_self`, `der_add`, `der_sub`, `der_smul` and `der_mul` with `@[simp]`. Each has the single side condition `D K F t ≠ 0`, which simp can discharge from `simp [hDt]`. They are terminating, since each rule strictly decreases the argument of `der`. `der_mul` produces only smaller `der` calls. Then `der_sum_smul`, `der_pow_two`, `wr_one_left`, `der_smul_sub_smul` and the `hDf` step in `evalAt_mul_inv_eq_evalAt_der` can become `simp [hDt]` (plus `ring` where needed). If conditional simp lemmas are unwanted globally, put them in a named simp set used as `simp [hDt, der_...]`. I have not checked that the discharger closes these side goals.
findings.benefit: Derivative computations on `der` (Wronskian and local-coordinate manipulations) would be automated and uniform, instead of chains of explicit `rw` with `hDt` threaded through. Downstream proofs would be shorter and less brittle to the order of rewrites.
